content: 1. Packing Instructions Overview: The annex outlines four specific packing instructions relevant to the transportation of infectious substances. These include P620, P650, and P621, which are derived from the UN Model Regulations, and an additional instruction (PI620/PI650) specific to air transport as per ICAO Technical Instructions. Notably, the fourth instruction has no equivalent in the UN Model Regulations. 2. Packing Instruction P620: This instruction applies to UN 2814 and UN 2900 substances. It mandates the use of a triple-layer packaging system: Inner Packaging: Leakproof primary receptacles. Leakproof secondary packaging. For liquid infectious substances, sufficient absorbent material must be placed between the primary and secondary layers to absorb the entire contents. If multiple fragile primary receptacles are used, they must be individually wrapped or separated to prevent contact. Outer Packaging: A rigid outer container is required, which may include drums, boxes, or jerricans. The smallest external dimension must be at least 100 mm (4 inches). Additional Requirements: Infectious substances must not be consolidated with unrelated goods unless necessary for maintaining viability, stability, or neutralizing hazards. For substances transported at ambient or elevated temperatures, primary receptacles must be made of glass, metal, or plastic with secure closures (e.g., heat seals, stoppers, or crimp seals). For refrigerated or frozen substances, interior supports must secure the secondary packaging after ice or dry ice dissipates. Leakproof outer packaging is required for ice, while dry ice packaging must allow carbon dioxide gas release. For substances transported in liquid nitrogen, primary and secondary receptacles must withstand extremely low temperatures. Lyophilized substances may be transported in flame-sealed glass ampoules or rubber-stoppered glass vials with metal seals. Packaging must withstand internal pressure differentials of at least 95 kPa and temperature ranges from -40°C to +55°C (-40°F to +130°F). 3. Packing Instruction P650: This instruction applies to UN 3373 substances and requires: Packaging of good quality and strength to withstand normal transport conditions, including shocks, vibrations, and environmental changes. A triple-layer system: Leakproof primary receptacles. Leakproof secondary packaging. Rigid outer packaging with cushioning material to prevent damage. Marking requirements: The outer packaging must display a diamond-shaped mark with specific dimensions and the proper shipping name, BIOLOGICAL SUBSTANCE, CATEGORY B, in letters at least 6 mm high. Drop Test: The package must withstand a 2-meter drop in any orientation without leakage. 4. Packing Instruction P621: This instruction applies to UN 3291 substances and requires: Sufficient absorbent material to retain all liquid contents. Packaging must conform to Packing Group II performance standards for solids or liquids, depending on the substance. Rigid outer packaging options include drums, boxes, or jerricans. 5. Packing Instruction PI954: This instruction applies to the air transport of UN 1845 (Carbon Dioxide, Solid or Dry Ice) and includes: Packaging must allow the release of carbon dioxide gas to prevent pressure buildup. The shipper must coordinate with the operator to ensure ventilation safety procedures are followed. Documentation requirements: The dangerous goods transport document is not required if alternative written documentation is provided, detailing the contents and quantities. The net mass of dry ice must be marked on the package exterior. 6. Export Regulations for Infectious Substances: CITES Compliance: If exporting infectious substances potentially covered under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES), an export permit must be obtained from the relevant governmental authority. This involves proving the material was legally obtained and that its export will not harm the species' survival. Both exporting and importing countries typically require permits. Nagoya Protocol Compliance: If the substances fall under the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) and the Nagoya Protocol, adherence to domestic and international regulations is required. This includes obtaining prior informed consent from the country providing the genetic resources and negotiating a Material Transfer Agreement (MTA) to ensure fair benefit-sharing. These detailed instructions and regulations ensure the safe and compliant transport of infectious substances, minimizing risks to public health and the environment.
